input.natural_language_query: According to the RFM definition document, calculate the average sales per order for each customer within distinct RFM segments, considering only 'delivered' orders. Use the customer unique identifier. Clearly define how to calculate Recency based on the latest purchase timestamp and specify the criteria for classifying RFM segments. The average sales should be computed as the total spend divided by the total number of orders. Please analyze and report the differences in average sales across the RFM segments

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH RecencyScore AS ( SELECT customer_unique_id, MAX(order_purchase_timestamp) AS last_purchase, NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY MAX(order_purchase_timestamp) DESC) AS recency FROM orders JOIN customers USING (customer_id) WHERE order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_unique_id ), FrequencyScore AS ( SELECT customer_unique_id, COUNT(order_id) AS total_orders, NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(order_id) DESC) AS frequency FROM orders JOIN customers USING (customer_id) WHERE order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_unique_id ), MonetaryScore AS ( SELECT customer_unique_id, SUM(price) AS total_spent, NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY SUM(price) DESC) AS monetary FROM orders JOIN order_items USING (order_id) JOIN customers USING (customer_id) WHERE order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_unique_id ), -- 2. Assign each customer to a group RFM AS ( SELECT last_purchase, total_orders, total_spent, CASE WHEN recency = 1 AND frequency + monetary IN (1, 2, 3, 4) THEN "Champions" WHEN recency IN (4, 5) AND frequency + monetary IN (1, 2) THEN "Can't Lose Them" WHEN recency IN (4, 5) AND frequency + monetary IN (3, 4, 5, 6) THEN "Hibernating" WHEN recency IN (4, 5) AND frequency + monetary IN (7, 8, 9, 10) THEN "Lost" WHEN recency IN (2, 3) AND frequency + monetary IN (1, 2, 3, 4) THEN "Loyal Customers" WHEN recency = 3 AND frequency + monetary IN (5, 6) THEN "Needs Attention" WHEN recency = 1 AND frequency + monetary IN (7, 8) THEN "Recent Users" WHEN recency = 1 AND frequency + monetary IN (5, 6) OR recency = 2 AND frequency + monetary IN (5, 6, 7, 8) THEN "Potentital Loyalists" WHEN recency = 1 AND frequency + monetary IN (9, 10) THEN "Price Sensitive" WHEN recency = 2 AND frequency + monetary IN (9, 10) THEN "Promising" WHEN recency = 3 AND frequency + monetary IN (7, 8, 9, 10) THEN "About to Sleep" END AS RFM_Bucket FROM RecencyScore JOIN FrequencyScore USING (customer_unique_id) JOIN MonetaryScore USING (customer_unique_id) ) SELECT RFM_Bucket, AVG(total_spent / total_orders) AS avg_sales_per_customer FROM RFM GROUP BY RFM_Bucket

searches.query: audience segmentation interest composition index digital marketing market concentration
searches.rationale: The question normalizes each interest by dividing composition by an index value and tracks which interest dominates each month, which mirrors the composition-index methodology used in audience measurement.
searches.context_summary: In audience measurement, the composition index expresses the concentration of a target group on a given site or ad network relative to that group's concentration across the total internet population. It is calculated by dividing the target's concentration percentage on a specific property by that same target's concentration across the entire internet and multiplying by 100, so an index of 200 means the audience is twice as concentrated as the baseline. Values above 100 indicate the target is over-represented and values below 100 indicate under-representation, which lets analysts rank which segments a property over-indexes on. High-composition placements carry fewer raw impressions but a higher concentration of the preferred target, giving advertisers higher-quality reach. Tracking which interest holds the highest composition month over month therefore captures shifts in audience concentration rather than raw popularity. This normalization is the standard way to distinguish a genuinely dominant, over-indexed interest from one that merely has a large but diffuse base.

searches.rationale: The question hinges on comparing users with positive versus zero engagement time across two windows, so the GA4 definition of engagement time is the core background.
searches.context_summary: GA4 defines user engagement as the amount of time a user spends with a web page in focus or an app screen in the foreground. The platform records session time in milliseconds and transmits it when the user backgrounds the app, shifts focus away from the page, navigates away, or the app crashes, attaching the accumulated value to the next event as the engagement_time_msec parameter. This timing data feeds reporting metrics such as User engagement and Average engagement time. Because engagement time is only recorded when a user actively interacts, a user can register positive engagement time in a longer window while showing no engagement in a shorter, more recent window, which is the behavioral signature of a user who has gone dormant. This makes engagement_time_msec the natural basis for set-difference style analyses that isolate previously engaged users who stopped interacting, supporting churn and re-engagement interpretations.

input.natural_language_query: According to the RFM definition document, calculate the average sales per order for each customer within distinct RFM segments, considering only 'delivered' orders. Use the customer unique identifier. Clearly define how to calculate Recency based on the latest purchase timestamp and specify the criteria for classifying RFM segments. The average sales should be computed as the total spend divided by the total number of orders. Please analyze and report the differences in average sales across the RFM segments

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH RecencyScore AS ( SELECT customer_unique_id, MAX(order_purchase_timestamp) AS last_purchase, NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY MAX(order_purchase_timestamp) DESC) AS recency FROM orders JOIN customers USING (customer_id) WHERE order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_unique_id ), FrequencyScore AS ( SELECT customer_unique_id, COUNT(order_id) AS total_orders, NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(order_id) DESC) AS frequency FROM orders JOIN customers USING (customer_id) WHERE order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_unique_id ), MonetaryScore AS ( SELECT customer_unique_id, SUM(price) AS total_spent, NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY SUM(price) DESC) AS monetary FROM orders JOIN order_items USING (order_id) JOIN customers USING (customer_id) WHERE order_status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_unique_id ), -- 2. Assign each customer to a group RFM AS ( SELECT last_purchase, total_orders, total_spent, CASE WHEN recency = 1 AND frequency + monetary IN (1, 2, 3, 4) THEN "Champions" WHEN recency IN (4, 5) AND frequency + monetary IN (1, 2) THEN "Can't Lose Them" WHEN recency IN (4, 5) AND frequency + monetary IN (3, 4, 5, 6) THEN "Hibernating" WHEN recency IN (4, 5) AND frequency + monetary IN (7, 8, 9, 10) THEN "Lost" WHEN recency IN (2, 3) AND frequency + monetary IN (1, 2, 3, 4) THEN "Loyal Customers" WHEN recency = 3 AND frequency + monetary IN (5, 6) THEN "Needs Attention" WHEN recency = 1 AND frequency + monetary IN (7, 8) THEN "Recent Users" WHEN recency = 1 AND frequency + monetary IN (5, 6) OR recency = 2 AND frequency + monetary IN (5, 6, 7, 8) THEN "Potentital Loyalists" WHEN recency = 1 AND frequency + monetary IN (9, 10) THEN "Price Sensitive" WHEN recency = 2 AND frequency + monetary IN (9, 10) THEN "Promising" WHEN recency = 3 AND frequency + monetary IN (7, 8, 9, 10) THEN "About to Sleep" END AS RFM_Bucket FROM RecencyScore JOIN FrequencyScore USING (customer_unique_id) JOIN MonetaryScore USING (customer_unique_id) ) SELECT RFM_Bucket, AVG(total_spent / total_orders) AS avg_sales_per_customer FROM RFM GROUP BY RFM_Bucket

searches.context_summary: RFM segmentation scores each customer on Recency (how recently they bought), Frequency (how often), and Monetary value (how much they spend), typically on a 1-to-5 scale, and maps the score combinations to named behavioral segments. A standard framework defines Champions as buyers who purchased very recently, shop frequently, and have the highest value; Loyal Customers as high spenders visiting regularly and next in value; Potential Loyalists as recent buyers with modest but growing spend; and Promising as recent buyers with low frequency and monetary scores. Lower-engagement segments include Needs Attention and At Risk (mid-value customers whose visit cadence is lapsing), Can't Lose Them (formerly high-spending regulars who have disengaged and carry high win-back priority), and Hibernating (low-spend customers who have not purchased recently). Because segments are defined jointly by recency, frequency, and monetary dimensions rather than by monetary value alone, average sales per order does not move monotonically with loyalty ranking, and monetary is not redundant with the other two axes. Strategically, the top segments (Champions, Loyal) are retention and upsell priorities while lower-value or lapsing segments are candidates for reactivation or differentiated engagement, which supports portfolio-based rather than linear interpretations of the segment sales differences.

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH product_viewed AS ( SELECT t1.page_id, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_page_views, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_added_to_cart FROM shopping_cart_page_hierarchy AS t1 JOIN shopping_cart_events AS t2 ON t1.page_id = t2.page_id WHERE t1.product_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY t1.page_id ), product_purchased AS ( SELECT t2.page_id, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchased_from_cart FROM shopping_cart_page_hierarchy AS t1 JOIN shopping_cart_events AS t2 ON t1.page_id = t2.page_id WHERE t1.product_id IS NOT NULL AND EXISTS ( SELECT visit_id FROM shopping_cart_events WHERE event_type = 3 AND t2.visit_id = visit_id ) AND t1.page_id NOT IN (1, 2, 12, 13) GROUP BY t2.page_id ), product_abandoned AS ( SELECT t2.page_id, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS abandoned_in_cart FROM shopping_cart_page_hierarchy AS t1 JOIN shopping_cart_events AS t2 ON t1.page_id = t2.page_id WHERE t1.product_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS ( SELECT visit_id FROM shopping_cart_events WHERE event_type = 3 AND t2.visit_id = visit_id ) AND t1.page_id NOT IN (1, 2, 12, 13) GROUP BY t2.page_id ) SELECT t1.page_id, t1.page_name, t2.n_page_views AS 'number of product being viewed', t2.n_added_to_cart AS 'number added to the cart', t4.abandoned_in_cart AS 'without being purchased in cart', t3.purchased_from_cart AS 'count of actual purchases' FROM shopping_cart_page_hierarchy AS t1 JOIN product_viewed AS t2 ON t2.page_id = t1.page_id JOIN product_purchased AS t3 ON t3.page_id = t1.page_id JOIN product_abandoned AS t4 ON t4.page_id = t1.page_id;

searches.context_summary: Monthly Average Balance (MAB) is defined as the average closing balance in a bank account over one month, computed as the sum of daily closing balances divided by the number of days in the month. The article walks through an example where varying daily balances totaling Rs 3,80,000 across 30 days yield an MAB of about Rs 12,667, illustrating that MAB is time-averaged rather than a single point-in-time figure. Banks require MAB because it evidences a regular, steady source of income and stable spending patterns, and the minimum-balance requirement also generates revenue that funds premium services such as spending analytics, payroll processing, and forex. MAB is distinguished from a minimum balance, which is the lowest amount held at any point, whereas MAB reflects activity throughout the month. This clarifies why a methodology that instead measures balance as of the 1st of each month and floors negatives at zero differs fundamentally from standard time-averaged MAB and speaks to conservative liquidity planning. Published June 5, 2024.

searches.rationale: The question interprets declining monthly maximum 30-day rolling average balances as signals of customer behavior and risk, so background on rolling-balance feature engineering and risk segmentation in banking is relevant.

Complementary retail-banking practice uses profiling scorecards where average balance is treated as a clear reflection of the strength of the bank-client relationship, followed by K-Means segmentation to build risk tiers and targeted product strategies for retention, cost reduction, and credit-quality-based risk mitigation. searches.query: average daily balance method credit card calculation definition
searches.rationale: Multiple options explicitly compare the carry-forward daily-balance methodology to the credit card average daily balance technique, so a precise definition of that method is required.
searches.context_summary: The average daily balance (ADB) method is a technique for calculating interest charged on an outstanding balance and is most commonly employed by credit card issuers to compute finance charges. It sums the balance held on each calendar day of the billing cycle and divides by the number of days, so it naturally accommodates fluctuating balances by tracking the specific balance for each day as purchases and payments occur. Finance charges follow the formula (APR x days in billing cycle x average daily balance) / 365; the article's example yields a $264 average daily balance producing $2.71 in interest at 15% APR over 25 days. Because early payments and delayed purchases lower the average daily balance, the method rewards timing behavior. This directly grounds the comparison in the question: the analyzed methodology mirrors the credit-card daily-balance carry-forward approach but substitutes monthly maximum aggregation for averaging, which points toward peak-liquidity or credit-exposure monitoring rather than standard interest averaging. Published November 26, 2020.

searches.rationale: The task breaks down views, add-to-cart, cart-without-purchase, and purchases for luxury food products, so industry cart-abandonment benchmarks (especially luxury) provide the real-world context for interpreting abandonment patterns.
searches.context_summary: As of October 2024, the average online cart abandonment rate across all industries was 74.09%, but rates vary sharply by category. Luxury and jewelry had the highest abandonment at 82.84%, meaning more than four in five shoppers who added items left without buying, followed by beauty and personal care at 80.92%, home and furniture at 80.32%, and fashion/apparel at 78.53%. Food and beverage abandonment was markedly lower at 63.62%, with consumer goods at 57.37% and pet care and veterinary services best at 54.78%. This roughly 28-percentage-point gap between luxury/jewelry and pet care illustrates how strongly shopper follow-through differs across product categories. For a portfolio of luxury food items this frames cart abandonment as a category-specific, high-consideration behavior rather than uniform noise, supporting interpretations that premium products carry distinct hesitation points requiring differentiated conversion optimization. searches.query: interest based audience targeting composition index digital marketing definition
searches.rationale: The question ranks interest categories by composition value and analyzes market concentration for interest-based targeting, so the definition and meaning of the composition index metric is the core background needed.
searches.context_summary: Composition measures the concentration of a particular target group of consumers on a given website or ad network compared to that target's concentration in the total internet population. The composition index is computed by dividing the target audience's percentage on a specific site by their percentage in the overall internet population and multiplying by 100; for example, 50% of a site's visitors in the target versus 25% of all internet users gives a 200 index. An index above 100 means the target is overrepresented on that property, below 100 means underrepresented, and 100 means alignment with the general internet. The article argues that a page-views-based composition index better predicts actual ad exposure than a visitor-based one, since ads are placed on pages. This grounds the interpretation of high versus low composition values across interest categories: high-composition categories represent concentrated, well-targeted audiences valuable for advertisers, while low-composition ones are more diffuse, matching the question's contrast between concentrated luxury interest categories and dispersed entertainment ones. Published March 16, 2011.

searches.query: Makarov Schoar trading and arbitrage in cryptocurrency markets regional price differences capital controls
searches.rationale: The question concerns regional Bitcoin average purchase-price differences and cross-market dynamics, so I searched for the foundational research on cross-country crypto arbitrage and price premia.
searches.context_summary: The Makarov and Schoar study Trading and Arbitrage in Cryptocurrency Markets, summarized on the Harvard Law School Forum on September 21, 2019, documents large, recurrent arbitrage opportunities in bitcoin prices across exchanges that can persist for weeks. Price deviations between exchanges within the same country typically do not exceed about 1 percent, whereas cross-border spreads can be dramatic; the Kimchi premium between US and Korean exchanges reached 40 percent during December 2017 to February 2018, representing roughly $2 billion in unrealized arbitrage. Outside the US and Europe, bitcoin consistently trades at a premium and rarely falls below US prices, an asymmetry that widens during periods of strong global demand and bitcoin appreciation. The authors attribute persistent cross-country spreads primarily to capital controls and weaker financial institutions, noting that arbitrage spreads between different cryptocurrencies on the same exchange are an order of magnitude smaller than spreads relative to fiat. Price deviations across countries co-move and open up in times of large bitcoin appreciation, indicating integrated global dynamics layered over persistent regional differences. This context supports interpreting regional differences in average purchase price as reflecting genuine market microstructure, local demand, and regulatory frictions rather than mere statistical noise, while acknowledging increasing global market integration.

Refugee figures are incorporated for some countries. These methodological distinctions explain why country-specific notes vary across Latin America and the Caribbean, including the use of foreign-born versus nationality-based estimates and refugee-data enhancements, and they define the criteria of comparability, source consistency, and definitional alignment relevant to assessing reliability and policy implications.

searches.context_summary: After independence in 1962, Algeria treated education as central to modernization, having inherited very low literacy of only about 10 percent among indigenous Algerians. The government established centralized, compulsory schooling for ages 6 to 15 and, by the 1970s, devoted roughly one-third of the state budget to education, securing five World Bank loans between 1973 and 1980 to fund expansion (POMEPS Studies 31, October 2018). Overall enrollment rose from 47.2 percent in 1966 to 70.4 percent in 1977 and 79.86 percent in 1987, while total student numbers grew from 940,000 in 1962 toward millions by the late 1990s, even as the population more than doubled between 1970 and 1990. Arabization of the primary curriculum, replacing French with Arabic, was a defining early policy begun in 1963 to 1964 (Education in Algeria, Wikipedia). These figures bracket the 1975 to 1980 window and indicate primary enrollment in the mid-to-high 70s percent, consistent with a period of rapid, budget-backed post-independence educational expansion. This context supports reading a roughly 76.8 percent average adjusted net primary enrolment rate as evidence of successful expansion during post-colonial reconstruction, while cautioning against over-claiming precision or regional-benchmark superiority from a single figure.

input.natural_language_query: For account type H and the MCC description: Eating Places and Restaurants, what would be the average fee that the card scheme GlobalCard would charge for a transaction value of 10 EUR? Provide the answer in EUR and 6 decimals

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH target_mcc AS ( -- Find the MCC for "Eating Places and Restaurants" SELECT mcc FROM merchant_category_codes WHERE description = 'Eating Places and Restaurants' ), applicable_fees AS ( -- Find all fees for GlobalCard that apply to account type H and our target MCC SELECT DISTINCT f.fixed_amount, f.rate FROM fees f CROSS JOIN target_mcc tm WHERE f.card_scheme = 'GlobalCard' AND f.fixed_amount IS NOT NULL AND f.rate IS NOT NULL -- Check if fee applies to account type H AND ( -- Either no account type restriction (applies to all) NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_account_types fat WHERE fat.fee_id = f.id) OR -- Or explicitly includes account type H EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_account_types fat WHERE fat.fee_id = f.id AND fat.account_type = 'H') ) -- Check if fee applies to our target MCC AND ( -- Either no MCC restriction (applies to all) NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_merchant_category_codes fmcc WHERE fmcc.fee_id = f.id) OR -- Or explicitly includes our target MCC EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_merchant_category_codes fmcc WHERE fmcc.fee_id = f.id AND fmcc.mcc = tm.mcc) ) ), calculated_fees AS ( -- Calculate the fee for 10 EUR transaction SELECT (fixed_amount + rate * 10.0 / 10000.0) as fee FROM applicable_fees ) SELECT PRINTF('%.6f', AVG(fee)) as average_fee FROM calculated_fees;

searches.context_summary: The EU Interchange Fee Regulation caps interchange at 0.3 percent of transaction value for consumer credit cards and 0.2 percent for consumer debit cards, in force since December 2015, with member states allowed to set lower caps. Scheme fees paid to the card network are a separate layer, typically on the order of 0.05 percent to 0.15 percent, distinct from interchange and from acquirer markup. Corporate cards, three-party schemes such as Amex and Diners, and ATM transactions are exempt from the caps. The regulation's aim is transparency and competition so merchants can see the fee layers they pay. Against this baseline, an effective rate near 1.23 percent sits well above pure scheme-assessment levels and above capped consumer interchange, consistent with the options that read the figure as a blended or composite merchant-facing rate rather than a single scheme-assessment component.

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH target_mcc AS ( -- Find the MCC for "Eating Places and Restaurants" SELECT mcc FROM merchant_category_codes WHERE description = 'Eating Places and Restaurants' ), applicable_fees AS ( -- Find all fees for GlobalCard that apply to account type H and our target MCC SELECT DISTINCT f.fixed_amount, f.rate FROM fees f CROSS JOIN target_mcc tm WHERE f.card_scheme = 'GlobalCard' AND f.fixed_amount IS NOT NULL AND f.rate IS NOT NULL -- Check if fee applies to account type H AND ( -- Either no account type restriction (applies to all) NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_account_types fat WHERE fat.fee_id = f.id) OR -- Or explicitly includes account type H EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_account_types fat WHERE fat.fee_id = f.id AND fat.account_type = 'H') ) -- Check if fee applies to our target MCC AND ( -- Either no MCC restriction (applies to all) NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_merchant_category_codes fmcc WHERE fmcc.fee_id = f.id) OR -- Or explicitly includes our target MCC EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_merchant_category_codes fmcc WHERE fmcc.fee_id = f.id AND fmcc.mcc = tm.mcc) ) ), calculated_fees AS ( -- Calculate the fee for 10 EUR transaction SELECT (fixed_amount + rate * 10.0 / 10000.0) as fee FROM applicable_fees ) SELECT PRINTF('%.6f', AVG(fee)) as average_fee FROM calculated_fees;

searches.context_summary: A 2024 study, 'Decentralized Finance and Local Public Goods: A Bayesian Maximum Entropy Model of School District Spending in the U.S.' (Melo, arXiv:2404.17700, submitted April 2024), analyzes U.S. school district expenditures from 2000 to 2016 through the Tiebout hypothesis, in which households vote with their feet and sort across jurisdictions by their willingness and ability to pay for local public goods such as K-12 education. Using a Bayesian maximum entropy model, it finds district spending distributions are sharply peaked and positively skewed, which the author reads as evidence of socioeconomic stratification driven by inter-jurisdictional competition and household choice. Under Tiebout sorting, local governments compete to deliver desired services at least cost or lose residents and their tax dollars, producing differentiated budgeting and investment responses to local fiscal conditions. This framework directly informs interpreting school-level budgeted versus invested amounts as strategic positioning within a competitive educational-finance market rather than as isolated budget variance.

searches.query: Show each school name, its budgeted amount, and invested amount in year 2002 or after.

input.natural_language_query: Identify the difference in the number of the oldest and youngest users registered between January 1, 2019, and April 30, 2022, from our e-commerce platform data.

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH youngest AS ( SELECT "gender", "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age", 'youngest' AS "tag" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" WHERE "age" = (SELECT MIN("age") FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS") AND TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2022-04-30') GROUP BY "gender", "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" ORDER BY "gender" ), oldest AS ( SELECT "gender", "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age", 'oldest' AS "tag" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" WHERE "age" = (SELECT MAX("age") FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS") AND TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2022-04-30') GROUP BY "gender", "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" ORDER BY "gender" ), TEMP_record AS ( SELECT * FROM youngest UNION ALL SELECT * FROM oldest ) SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN "age" = (SELECT MAX("age") FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS") THEN 1 END) - SUM(CASE WHEN "age" = (SELECT MIN("age") FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS") THEN 1 END) AS "diff" FROM TEMP_record;

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: with page_visit_sequence AS ( SELECT fullVisitorID, visitID, pagePath, LEAD(timestamp, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY fullVisitorId, visitID order by timestamp) - timestamp AS page_duration, LEAD(pagePath, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY fullVisitorId, visitID order by timestamp) AS next_page, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY fullVisitorId, visitID order by timestamp) AS step_number FROM ( SELECT pages.fullVisitorID, pages.visitID, pages.pagePath, visitors.campaign, MIN(pages.timestamp) timestamp FROM ( SELECT fullVisitorId, visitId, trafficSource.campaign campaign FROM `bigquery-public-data.google_analytics_sample.ga_sessions_*`, UNNEST(hits) as hits WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20170101' AND '20170131' AND hits.type='PAGE' AND REGEXP_CONTAINS(hits.page.pagePath, r'^/home') AND REGEXP_CONTAINS(trafficSource.campaign, r'Data Share') ) AS visitors JOIN( SELECT fullVisitorId, visitId, visitStartTime + hits.time / 1000 AS timestamp, hits.page.pagePath AS pagePath FROM `bigquery-public-data.google_analytics_sample.ga_sessions_*`, UNNEST(hits) as hits WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20170101' AND '20170131' ) as pages ON visitors.fullVisitorID = pages.fullVisitorID AND visitors.visitID = pages.visitID GROUP BY pages.fullVisitorID, visitors.campaign, pages.visitID, pages.pagePath ORDER BY pages.fullVisitorID, pages.visitID, timestamp ) ORDER BY fullVisitorId, visitID, step_number ), most_common_next_page AS ( SELECT next_page, COUNT(next_page) as page_count FROM page_visit_sequence WHERE next_page IS NOT NULL AND REGEXP_CONTAINS(pagePath, r'^/home') GROUP BY next_page ORDER BY page_count DESC LIMIT 1 ), max_page_duration AS ( SELECT MAX(page_duration) as max_duration FROM page_visit_sequence WHERE page_duration IS NOT NULL AND REGEXP_CONTAINS(pagePath, r'^/home') ) SELECT next_page, max_duration FROM most_common_next_page, max_page_duration;

searches.rationale: Several answer options tie the April drop in monthly maximum balances to early-pandemic customer financial stability, so real-world context on early-2020 bank balance and deposit dynamics is needed to weigh those claims.
searches.context_summary: In early 2020, U.S. bank customer balances shifted sharply as companies drew down credit lines, federal stimulus flowed in, and consumer spending slowed; the personal savings rate jumped from roughly 8 percent to nearly 35 percent in April 2020. Aggregate deposits at all U.S. banks rose more than 20 percent in 2020, versus 4.7 percent the prior year, and deposit growth began to outpace loans at the start of 2020. Banks responded to the uncertainty by retaining large liquid-asset buffers rather than deploying the inflows. Institutions with weaker pre-pandemic liquidity coverage were more likely to borrow from the Federal Reserve discount window in early 2020. This backdrop shows that the first months of 2020 were a period of genuine customer-behavior and liquidity dislocation, giving real-world grounding for interpreting a February-to-April balance decline as an early-pandemic effect rather than routine seasonality. It also cautions that system-wide balances actually surged in this window, so any per-customer peak-balance decline reflects a specific portfolio, not the macro trend.

searches.query: 30-day rolling average balance liquidity risk management banking methodology
searches.rationale: The task computes a 30-day rolling-average balance as a risk lens, so grounding the 30-day horizon in standard bank liquidity-risk practice clarifies whether such a metric is a recognized risk-assessment tool.
searches.context_summary: A 30-day horizon is central to bank liquidity risk management: the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio measures a bank's high-quality liquid assets against projected net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period. Supervisory guidance frames short-term liquidity within a 12-month view, with cumulative surplus or deficit forecasts at 30-, 90-, and 180-day points, because liquidity crises can be rapid short-term shocks or slower intermediate tightening. Net outflows are estimated by applying run-off rates to different funding sources net of expected inflows over the chosen window. This establishes that a rolling 30-day balance is a legitimate risk-assessment construct rather than an arbitrary smoothing choice. However, these frameworks operate at the institution and portfolio level on outflows and liquid assets, not on per-customer running balances, so mapping the dataset's per-customer 30-day averages directly onto regulatory liquidity metrics is an analogy, not an identity.

searches.rationale: The task's core computation, dividing composition by index value to get average composition and tracking the monthly maximum and its rolling average, is defined by the Fresh Segments interest-metrics dataset, so grounding those metric definitions is essential.
searches.context_summary: Fresh Segments aggregates each client's customer interest activity into a monthly interest_metrics dataset with columns for _month, _year, month_year, interest_id, composition, index_value, ranking, and percentile_ranking. The composition metric is the percentage of a client's customer list that interacted with online assets tied to a given interest in a month (for example, 11.89 means 11.89 percent interacted with interest 32486 in July 2018). The index_value expresses that interest's composition relative to the average composition across all Fresh Segments clients, so an index of 6.19 means the interest's composition is 6.19 times the cross-client average. Average composition is therefore recovered by dividing composition by index_value, rounded to two decimals, which is exactly the max index composition the task computes per month before taking a three-month rolling average. Interest names in the data include specific travel and niche audience segments, matching the interest labels referenced in the options. This grounds the methodology as an established audience-composition indexing approach where composition-to-index ratios normalize an interest's popularity against a benchmark population, supporting interpretations that treat the ratios as a legitimate market-dynamics signal rather than random reporting noise. gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: with page_visit_sequence AS ( SELECT fullVisitorID, visitID, pagePath, LEAD(timestamp, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY fullVisitorId, visitID order by timestamp) - timestamp AS page_duration, LEAD(pagePath, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY fullVisitorId, visitID order by timestamp) AS next_page, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY fullVisitorId, visitID order by timestamp) AS step_number FROM ( SELECT pages.fullVisitorID, pages.visitID, pages.pagePath, visitors.campaign, MIN(pages.timestamp) timestamp FROM ( SELECT fullVisitorId, visitId, trafficSource.campaign campaign FROM `bigquery-public-data.google_analytics_sample.ga_sessions_*`, UNNEST(hits) as hits WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20170101' AND '20170131' AND hits.type='PAGE' AND REGEXP_CONTAINS(hits.page.pagePath, r'^/home') AND REGEXP_CONTAINS(trafficSource.campaign, r'Data Share') ) AS visitors JOIN( SELECT fullVisitorId, visitId, visitStartTime + hits.time / 1000 AS timestamp, hits.page.pagePath AS pagePath FROM `bigquery-public-data.google_analytics_sample.ga_sessions_*`, UNNEST(hits) as hits WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20170101' AND '20170131' ) as pages ON visitors.fullVisitorID = pages.fullVisitorID AND visitors.visitID = pages.visitID GROUP BY pages.fullVisitorID, visitors.campaign, pages.visitID, pages.pagePath ORDER BY pages.fullVisitorID, pages.visitID, timestamp ) ORDER BY fullVisitorId, visitID, step_number ), most_common_next_page AS ( SELECT next_page, COUNT(next_page) as page_count FROM page_visit_sequence WHERE next_page IS NOT NULL AND REGEXP_CONTAINS(pagePath, r'^/home') GROUP BY next_page ORDER BY page_count DESC LIMIT 1 ), max_page_duration AS ( SELECT MAX(page_duration) as max_duration FROM page_visit_sequence WHERE page_duration IS NOT NULL AND REGEXP_CONTAINS(pagePath, r'^/home') ) SELECT next_page, max_duration FROM most_common_next_page, max_page_duration;

searches.context_summary: This article on probabilistic customer lifetime value modeling (published February 16, 2022) explains the BG/NBD model developed by Fader, Hardie and Lee in 2005 for non-contractual, repeat-purchase businesses such as e-commerce. The model combines a Beta-Geometric distribution for customer churn with a Negative Binomial distribution for purchase frequency, and it explicitly captures customer heterogeneity through a Gamma distribution for purchase-rate variation and a Beta distribution for deactivation-probability variation. Each customer is assumed to follow a Poisson purchase process with an individual rate and can permanently deactivate after any transaction, so different customers exhibit fundamentally different transaction patterns. Predictions require only recency, frequency, and customer age rather than exact transaction timestamps. The authors argue these probabilistic models forecast future transactions more accurately than simple historical-frequency heuristics. This provides the CLV and buyer-heterogeneity framing referenced when interpreting early engagement (staying more than five minutes) as a leading indicator of later multi-session purchase behavior.

searches.context_summary: The Tax Foundation's global excise tax review (published April 7, 2023, updated September 25, 2024) identifies tobacco, alcohol, and motor fuels as the traditional targets of selective, or excise, taxation. Excise taxes are levied either per unit as specific or ad quantum taxes (a fixed amount per cigarette pack or gallon of fuel) or ad valorem as a percentage of the product's price or value. The report explains that basic economics dictates that as tax-induced prices rise, legal consumption of these goods falls, which is why governments use excise taxes both to raise revenue and to curb consumption of harmful goods. For heavily taxed products such as cigarettes, high rates create substitution effects and incentivize illicit or cross-border purchasing that grows significantly with the tax rate. The report also notes that the tax base for these traditional excise categories is shrinking over time. This background supports interpreting a product category that carries the highest effective tax rate as a selectively taxed category such as tobacco or alcohol, where transaction size and quantity patterns can reflect tax-aware buying behavior rather than random purchasing.

GROUP BY user_pseudo_id, user_active_date ), -- Create a table of the earliest quickplay event date for each user within the specified date range event_table AS ( SELECT user_pseudo_id, event_name, MIN(PARSE_DATE('%Y%m%d', `event_date`)) AS event_cohort_date FROM `firebase-public-project.analytics_153293282.events_*` WHERE event_name IN ('level_start_quickplay', 'level_end_quickplay', 'level_complete_quickplay', 'level_fail_quickplay', 'level_reset_quickplay', 'level_retry_quickplay') AND PARSE_DATE('%Y%m%d', `event_date`) BETWEEN (SELECT start_date FROM dates) AND (SELECT end_date FROM dates) GROUP BY user_pseudo_id, event_name ), -- Calculate the number of days since each user's initial quickplay event days_since_event_table AS ( SELECT events.user_pseudo_id, events.event_name AS event_cohort, events.event_cohort_date, days.user_active_date, DATE_DIFF(days.user_active_date, events.event_cohort_date, DAY) AS days_since_event FROM event_table events LEFT JOIN dates_active_table days ON events.user_pseudo_id = days.user_pseudo_id WHERE events.event_cohort_date <= days.user_active_date ), -- Calculate the weeks since each user's initial quickplay event and count the active days in each week weeks_retention AS ( SELECT event_cohort, user_pseudo_id, CAST(CASE WHEN days_since_event = 0 THEN 0 ELSE CEIL(days_since_event / 7) END AS INTEGER) AS weeks_since_event, COUNT(DISTINCT days_since_event) AS days_active_since_event -- Count Days Active in Week FROM days_since_event_table GROUP BY event_cohort, user_pseudo_id, weeks_since_event ), -- Aggregate the weekly retention data aggregated_weekly_retention_table AS ( SELECT event_cohort, weeks_since_event, SUM(days_active_since_event) AS weekly_days_active, COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS retained_users FROM weeks_retention GROUP BY event_cohort, weeks_since_event ), RETENTION_INFO AS ( SELECT event_cohort, weeks_since_event, weekly_days_active, retained_users, (retained_users / MAX(retained_users) OVER (PARTITION BY event_cohort)) AS retention_rate FROM aggregated_weekly_retention_table ORDER BY event_cohort, weeks_since_event ) SELECT event_cohort, retention_rate FROM RETENTION_INFO WHERE weeks_since_event = 2

input.natural_language_query: For account type H and the MCC description: Eating Places and Restaurants, what would be the average fee that the card scheme GlobalCard would charge for a transaction value of 10 EUR? Provide the answer in EUR and 6 decimals

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH target_mcc AS ( -- Find the MCC for "Eating Places and Restaurants" SELECT mcc FROM merchant_category_codes WHERE description = 'Eating Places and Restaurants' ), applicable_fees AS ( -- Find all fees for GlobalCard that apply to account type H and our target MCC SELECT DISTINCT f.fixed_amount, f.rate FROM fees f CROSS JOIN target_mcc tm WHERE f.card_scheme = 'GlobalCard' AND f.fixed_amount IS NOT NULL AND f.rate IS NOT NULL -- Check if fee applies to account type H AND ( -- Either no account type restriction (applies to all) NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_account_types fat WHERE fat.fee_id = f.id) OR -- Or explicitly includes account type H EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_account_types fat WHERE fat.fee_id = f.id AND fat.account_type = 'H') ) -- Check if fee applies to our target MCC AND ( -- Either no MCC restriction (applies to all) NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_merchant_category_codes fmcc WHERE fmcc.fee_id = f.id) OR -- Or explicitly includes our target MCC EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_merchant_category_codes fmcc WHERE fmcc.fee_id = f.id AND fmcc.mcc = tm.mcc) ) ), calculated_fees AS ( -- Calculate the fee for 10 EUR transaction SELECT (fixed_amount + rate * 10.0 / 10000.0) as fee FROM applicable_fees ) SELECT PRINTF('%.6f', AVG(fee)) as average_fee FROM calculated_fees;

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH target_mcc AS ( -- Find the MCC for "Eating Places and Restaurants" SELECT mcc FROM merchant_category_codes WHERE description = 'Eating Places and Restaurants' ), applicable_fees AS ( -- Find all fees for GlobalCard that apply to account type H and our target MCC SELECT DISTINCT f.fixed_amount, f.rate FROM fees f CROSS JOIN target_mcc tm WHERE f.card_scheme = 'GlobalCard' AND f.fixed_amount IS NOT NULL AND f.rate IS NOT NULL -- Check if fee applies to account type H AND ( -- Either no account type restriction (applies to all) NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_account_types fat WHERE fat.fee_id = f.id) OR -- Or explicitly includes account type H EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_account_types fat WHERE fat.fee_id = f.id AND fat.account_type = 'H') ) -- Check if fee applies to our target MCC AND ( -- Either no MCC restriction (applies to all) NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_merchant_category_codes fmcc WHERE fmcc.fee_id = f.id) OR -- Or explicitly includes our target MCC EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fees_merchant_category_codes fmcc WHERE fmcc.fee_id = f.id AND fmcc.mcc = tm.mcc) ) ), calculated_fees AS ( -- Calculate the fee for 10 EUR transaction SELECT (fixed_amount + rate * 10.0 / 10000.0) as fee FROM applicable_fees ) SELECT PRINTF('%.6f', AVG(fee)) as average_fee FROM calculated_fees;

input.natural_language_query: During the first half of 2017, focusing on hits product revenue, which traffic source generated the highest total product revenue, and what were the maximum daily, weekly, and monthly product revenues (in millions) for that top-performing source over this period?

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: DECLARE start_date STRING DEFAULT '20170101'; DECLARE end_date STRING DEFAULT '20170630'; WITH daily_revenue AS ( SELECT trafficSource.source AS source, date, SUM(productRevenue) / 1000000 AS revenue FROM `bigquery-public-data.google_analytics_sample.ga_sessions_*`, UNNEST (hits) AS hits, UNNEST (hits.product) AS product WHERE _table_suffix BETWEEN start_date AND end_date GROUP BY source, date ), weekly_revenue AS ( SELECT source, CONCAT(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM (PARSE_DATE('%Y%m%d', date))), 'W', EXTRACT(WEEK FROM (PARSE_DATE('%Y%m%d', date)))) AS week, SUM(revenue) AS revenue FROM daily_revenue GROUP BY source, week ), monthly_revenue AS ( SELECT source, CONCAT(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM (PARSE_DATE('%Y%m%d', date))),'0', EXTRACT(MONTH FROM (PARSE_DATE('%Y%m%d', date)))) AS month, SUM(revenue) AS revenue FROM daily_revenue GROUP BY source, month ), top_source AS ( SELECT source, SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue FROM daily_revenue GROUP BY source ORDER BY total_revenue DESC LIMIT 1 ), max_revenues AS ( ( SELECT 'Daily' AS time_type, date AS time, source, MAX(revenue) AS max_revenue FROM daily_revenue WHERE source = (SELECT source FROM top_source) GROUP BY source, date ORDER BY max_revenue DESC LIMIT 1 ) UNION ALL ( SELECT 'Weekly' AS time_type, week AS time, source, MAX(revenue) AS max_revenue FROM weekly_revenue WHERE source = (SELECT source FROM top_source) GROUP BY source, week ORDER BY max_revenue DESC LIMIT 1 ) UNION ALL ( SELECT 'Monthly' AS time_type, month AS time, source, MAX(revenue) AS max_revenue FROM monthly_revenue WHERE source = (SELECT source FROM top_source) GROUP BY source, month ORDER BY max_revenue DESC LIMIT 1 ) ) SELECT max_revenue FROM max_revenues ORDER BY max_revenue DESC;

searches.query: macroscopic properties buyer-seller networks online marketplaces dark web fat-tailed preferential attachment
searches.rationale: The interpretation options invoke fat-tailed distributions, memory effects, and preferential attachment across 28 dark marketplaces, which points to a specific marketplace-network study.
searches.context_summary: A 2022 PNAS Nexus study, Macroscopic properties of buyer-seller networks in online marketplaces, analyzed roughly 245 million transactions worth about 16 billion USD across 28 dark web marketplaces (Bitcoin-based, unregulated) operating between 2011 and 2021, plus 144 product markets of one regulated e-commerce platform. Despite large differences in language, product type, lifetime, regulation, and technology, the study found strikingly consistent regularities: transaction amounts, number of transactions per user, interevent times, and time between first and last transaction all follow heavy, fat-tailed distributions spanning many orders of magnitude. The authors show that buyer memory and a preferential attachment mechanism are central to how buyer-seller networks form, with buyers gravitating toward established, highly active sellers and becoming less likely to try a new seller the more they have already tried. This memory effect was found to be weaker in commercial networks than in social networks. The parallels between illicit dark markets and mainstream e-commerce suggest broadly universal principles govern online marketplace dynamics. This literature grounds interpretations that read country-channel transaction concentration as reflecting fat-tailed heterogeneity, network effects, and reputation-driven preferential attachment rather than simple geographic aggregation.

searches.rationale: The options invoke cognitive-assessment research to judge whether board-type average scores are a sound effectiveness measure, so validity evidence for game-based cognitive scoring is the relevant background.
searches.context_summary: A 2020 PLOS One study validating a mobile game-based assessment of cognitive control (the CoCon game) in children and adolescents found that game-derived index scores correlate meaningfully with traditional neuropsychological tests, for example working memory in-game correlated with digit span (r = 0.458) and full-scale IQ (r = 0.445), and a cognitive-control index correlated with vocabulary (r = 0.359). The working-memory index discriminated high- from low-ability groups with an AUC of 0.821, exceeding the 0.70 threshold for strong discrimination, and the authors concluded the game was a reliable and valid measure of cognitive control comparable to lab-based tests even when completed at home. More broadly, validation research on game-based cognitive assessment shows correlations with standard measures typically in the low-to-medium range (roughly r = 0.3-0.7). This literature supports interpretations that treat raw average scores by board type as only one input, arguing that sound effectiveness measurement should incorporate validated cognitive-assessment frameworks, user profiling, engagement, and complexity-to-skill considerations rather than ranking board types on numeric averages alone.

searches.context_summary: Numeric describes balance sheet reconciliation as verifying that general ledger account balances match supporting documentation, forming a critical part of the month-end close that maintains accurate financial statements, detects errors before they compound, and supports GAAP and SOX Section 404 compliance. It rests on the accounting identity assets = liabilities + equity, with teams pulling the GL trial balance and comparing it against source documents through steps of identifying accounts, gathering documentation, comparing, investigating differences, adjusting the ledger, and documenting results. Trintech frames fluctuation (variance) analysis as comparing a current period's balances against a prior period to surface account fluctuations, requiring documented explanations for significant swings for internal control and audit purposes. Firms set dollar and percentage thresholds to flag material changes, and each company defines what counts as material differently. These reconciliation and flux-analysis practices are the accounting context behind period-end customer balance calculations. Neither source treats a month-end balance difference as a predictive model of customer lifetime value or churn, which distinguishes routine reconciliation from strategic behavioral inference.

searches.context_summary: A bank (account) reconciliation compares the cash balance on a company's balance sheet against the corresponding bank-statement amount, and the two typically differ because of timing items such as outstanding checks, deposits in transit, service fees, and interest income. The reconciliation process systematically identifies these differences, helps detect fraud and cash manipulation, and adjusts both the bank balance and the company's books for legitimate items not yet recorded. When completed correctly, the adjusted bank balance matches the adjusted book balance, confirming that the cash figure reported on the balance sheet is accurate and the financial position is properly represented. This periodic reconciliation is described as fundamental to maintaining reliable financial statements and stakeholder confidence. Financial close management generalizes this discipline to reconciling all balance-sheet accounts at designated period ends and maintaining supporting workpapers, which is exactly the 'financial close management' / month-end close reasoning invoked in options C, F, and H.

searches.query: liquidity ratios ability to meet short-term obligations definition current quick cash ratio
searches.rationale: Option C ties the monthly maximum-balance aggregation to liquidity metrics that assess a company's ability to meet short-term obligations, so a definition of liquidity ratios grounds that interpretation.
searches.context_summary: A liquidity ratio is a financial ratio used to determine a company's ability to pay its short-term debt obligations using its most accessible assets. The ratios place liquid assets in the numerator and current liabilities in the denominator; a value above 1.0 indicates the company can cover its obligations, while a value below 1.0 signals potential difficulty. The three principal liquidity ratios are the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities), the quick ratio (which excludes inventory and prepaid expenses), and the cash ratio (which counts only cash and marketable securities), in increasing order of stringency. These metrics assess a firm's capacity to meet short-term obligations, which is the precise framing option C uses when it maps the query's maximum daily balances and monthly liquidity totals onto financial-health monitoring.

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH product_viewed AS ( SELECT t1.page_id, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_page_views, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS n_added_to_cart FROM shopping_cart_page_hierarchy AS t1 JOIN shopping_cart_events AS t2 ON t1.page_id = t2.page_id WHERE t1.product_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY t1.page_id ), product_purchased AS ( SELECT t2.page_id, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchased_from_cart FROM shopping_cart_page_hierarchy AS t1 JOIN shopping_cart_events AS t2 ON t1.page_id = t2.page_id WHERE t1.product_id IS NOT NULL AND EXISTS ( SELECT visit_id FROM shopping_cart_events WHERE event_type = 3 AND t2.visit_id = visit_id ) AND t1.page_id NOT IN (1, 2, 12, 13) GROUP BY t2.page_id ), product_abandoned AS ( SELECT t2.page_id, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS abandoned_in_cart FROM shopping_cart_page_hierarchy AS t1 JOIN shopping_cart_events AS t2 ON t1.page_id = t2.page_id WHERE t1.product_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS ( SELECT visit_id FROM shopping_cart_events WHERE event_type = 3 AND t2.visit_id = visit_id ) AND t1.page_id NOT IN (1, 2, 12, 13) GROUP BY t2.page_id ) SELECT t1.page_id, t1.page_name, t2.n_page_views AS 'number of product being viewed', t2.n_added_to_cart AS 'number added to the cart', t4.abandoned_in_cart AS 'without being purchased in cart', t3.purchased_from_cart AS 'count of actual purchases' FROM shopping_cart_page_hierarchy AS t1 JOIN product_viewed AS t2 ON t2.page_id = t1.page_id JOIN product_purchased AS t3 ON t3.page_id = t1.page_id JOIN product_abandoned AS t4 ON t4.page_id = t1.page_id;

searches.context_summary: The International Development Association is the World Bank institution that provides concessional financing to the world's poorest countries, with eligibility determined primarily by gross national income per capita falling below an annually adjusted operational threshold. A total of 78 countries are currently eligible to receive IDA resources, distributed across Africa (40), East Asia (14), South Asia (5), Europe and Central Asia (4), Latin America and the Caribbean (10), and the Middle East and North Africa region (5). Some 'blend' countries are eligible for both IDA and IBRD lending because of their income levels and creditworthiness, and certain small island economies that cannot access commercial borrowing also qualify despite exceeding the income threshold. This defines the IDA 'lending category' that the query uses to select borrowing countries, and it frames the multilateral development-finance architecture the options discuss.

searches.context_summary: Under the World Bank Debtor Reporting System (DRS), established in 1951, all IBRD and IDA borrowers are obliged to report detailed loan-by-loan public and publicly guaranteed external debt, quarterly for new commitments and annually for transactions. The International Debt Statistics methodology combines these borrower reports with data from multilateral development banks and organizations such as the IMF, UNCTAD, OECD, and BIS, and it notes that some series, such as short-term external debt, are 'as reported by debtor countries or are estimates,' so estimation is an accepted part of the methodology where direct reporting is unavailable. The World Bank has run an upgraded data-quality effort that matches IDA-eligible economies' reported figures against G7 and Paris Club creditor records, achieving a 98 percent match rate and cutting the margin of error from about 10 points to two. The December 2024 International Debt Report adds that IDA-eligible countries' external debt rose to $1.1 trillion with record debt-service costs. Together these sources support reading estimation-based reporting as part of a standardized multilateral oversight and debt-transparency framework accommodating varying institutional capacity (options B and E), rather than as evidence of pure administrative failure (options A, C, H).

searches.query: World Bank international migrant stock SM.POP.TOTL methodology refugees foreign-born
searches.rationale: The query asks for SM.POP.TOTL series descriptions and the options hinge on how migrant-stock methodology blends foreign-born estimates, UNHCR refugee data, and model-based estimates.
searches.context_summary: The World Bank metadata glossary defines international migrant stock (SM.POP.TOTL) as the number of people at mid-year born in a country other than the one in which they live, and it states explicitly that the count also includes refugees. Methodologically, the basic data come mainly from population censuses in the decennial census rounds, supplemented by population registers and nationally representative surveys, and international migrants are equated with the foreign-born population wherever possible. Where foreign-born data are unavailable, data on the foreign (non-citizen) population are used as estimates, and where neither exists, model-based estimates are derived, so the per-country descriptions vary by data source. In most developed countries, refugees admitted for resettlement are routinely included in population counts. The series is compiled by the UN Population Division and published within the World Development Indicators. This grounds the reasoning that the many distinct methodological descriptions per country reflect a mix of census, register, foreign-born, foreign-population, and model sources, and that UNHCR-style refugee statistics are integrated with foreign-born estimates rather than tracked by a single uniform method.

input.natural_language_query: Please generate a report that, for each month in 2021, provides the number of orders, the number of unique purchasers, and the profit (calculated as the sum of product retail prices minus the sum of product costs), where the orders were placed during 2021 by users who registered in 2021 for inventory items created in 2021, and group the results by the users' country, product department, and product category.

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH orders_x_order_items AS ( SELECT orders.*, order_items."inventory_item_id", order_items."sale_price" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDERS" AS orders LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDER_ITEMS" AS order_items ON orders."order_id" = order_items."order_id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ), orders_x_inventory AS ( SELECT orders_x_order_items.*, inventory_items."product_category", inventory_items."product_department", inventory_items."product_retail_price", inventory_items."product_distribution_center_id", inventory_items."cost", distribution_centers."name" FROM orders_x_order_items LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."INVENTORY_ITEMS" AS inventory_items ON orders_x_order_items."inventory_item_id" = inventory_items."id" LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."DISTRIBUTION_CENTERS" AS distribution_centers ON inventory_items."product_distribution_center_id" = distribution_centers."id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(inventory_items."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ), orders_x_users AS ( SELECT orders_x_inventory.*, users."country" AS "users_country" FROM orders_x_inventory LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" AS users ON orders_x_inventory."user_id" = users."id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(users."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ) SELECT DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', TO_DATE(TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders_x_users."created_at" / 1000000))) AS "reporting_month", orders_x_users."users_country", orders_x_users."product_department", orders_x_users."product_category", COUNT(DISTINCT orders_x_users."order_id") AS "n_order", COUNT(DISTINCT orders_x_users."user_id") AS "n_purchasers", SUM(orders_x_users."product_retail_price") - SUM(orders_x_users."cost") AS "profit" FROM orders_x_users GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4 ORDER BY "reporting_month";

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH orders AS ( SELECT "order_id", "user_id", "created_at", DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ("delivered_at" / 1000000)) AS "delivery_month", -- Converting to timestamp "status" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDERS" ), order_items AS ( SELECT "order_id", "product_id", "sale_price" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDER_ITEMS" ), products AS ( SELECT "id", "cost" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."PRODUCTS" ), users AS ( SELECT "id", "traffic_source" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" ), filter_join AS ( SELECT orders."order_id", orders."user_id", order_items."product_id", orders."delivery_month", orders."status", order_items."sale_price", products."cost", users."traffic_source" FROM orders JOIN order_items ON orders."order_id" = order_items."order_id" JOIN products ON order_items."product_id" = products."id" JOIN users ON orders."user_id" = users."id" WHERE orders."status" = 'Complete' AND users."traffic_source" = 'Facebook' AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2022-07-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2023-11-30') -- Include July for calculation ), monthly_sales AS ( SELECT "delivery_month", "traffic_source", SUM("sale_price") AS "total_revenue", SUM("sale_price") - SUM("cost") AS "total_profit", COUNT(DISTINCT "product_id") AS "product_quantity", COUNT(DISTINCT "order_id") AS "orders_quantity", COUNT(DISTINCT "user_id") AS "users_quantity" FROM filter_join GROUP BY "delivery_month", "traffic_source" ) -- Filter to show only 8th month and onwards, but calculate using July SELECT current_month."delivery_month", COALESCE( current_month."total_profit" - previous_month."total_profit", 0 -- If there is no previous month (i.e. for 8 ), return 0 ) AS "profit_vs_prior_month" FROM monthly_sales AS current_month LEFT JOIN monthly_sales AS previous_month ON current_month."traffic_source" = previous_month."traffic_source" AND current_month."delivery_month" = DATEADD(MONTH, -1, previous_month."delivery_month") -- Correctly join to previous month WHERE current_month."delivery_month" >= '2022-08-01' -- Only show August and later data, but use July for calculation ORDER BY "profit_vs_prior_month" DESC LIMIT 5;

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH station_neighborhoods AS ( SELECT bs.station_id, bs.name AS station_name, nb.neighborhood FROM `bigquery-public-data.san_francisco.bikeshare_stations` bs JOIN bigquery-public-data.san_francisco_neighborhoods.boundaries nb ON ST_Intersects(ST_GeogPoint(bs.longitude, bs.latitude), nb.neighborhood_geom) ), neighborhood_crime_counts AS ( SELECT neighborhood, COUNT(*) AS crime_count FROM ( SELECT n.neighborhood FROM bigquery-public-data.san_francisco.sfpd_incidents i JOIN bigquery-public-data.san_francisco_neighborhoods.boundaries n ON ST_Intersects(ST_GeogPoint(i.longitude, i.latitude), n.neighborhood_geom) ) AS incident_neighborhoods GROUP BY neighborhood ) SELECT sn.neighborhood, COUNT(station_name) AS station_number, ANY_VALUE(ncc.crime_count) AS crime_number FROM station_neighborhoods sn JOIN neighborhood_crime_counts ncc ON sn.neighborhood = ncc.neighborhood GROUP BY sn.neighborhood ORDER BY crime_number ASC

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH d AS ( SELECT a."order_id", TO_CHAR(TO_TIMESTAMP(a."created_at" / 1000000.0), 'YYYY-MM') AS "month", -- TO_CHAR(TO_TIMESTAMP(a."created_at" / 1000000.0), 'YYYY') AS "year", -- b."product_id", b."sale_price", c."category", c."cost" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDERS" AS a JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDER_ITEMS" AS b ON a."order_id" = b."order_id" JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."PRODUCTS" AS c ON b."product_id" = c."id" WHERE a."status" = 'Complete' AND TO_TIMESTAMP(a."created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2023-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2023-12-31') AND c."category" = 'Sleep & Lounge' ), e AS ( SELECT "month", "year", "sale_price", "category", "cost", SUM("sale_price") OVER (PARTITION BY "month", "category") AS "TPV", SUM("cost") OVER (PARTITION BY "month", "category") AS "total_cost", COUNT(DISTINCT "order_id") OVER (PARTITION BY "month", "category") AS "TPO", SUM("sale_price" - "cost") OVER (PARTITION BY "month", "category") AS "total_profit", SUM(("sale_price" - "cost") / "cost") OVER (PARTITION BY "month", "category") AS "Profit_to_cost_ratio" FROM d ) SELECT DISTINCT "month", "category", "TPV", "total_cost", "TPO", "total_profit", "Profit_to_cost_ratio" FROM e ORDER BY "month";

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH main AS ( SELECT "id" AS "user_id", "email", "gender", "country", "traffic_source" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-12-31') ), daate AS ( SELECT "user_id", "order_id", CAST(TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) AS DATE) AS "order_date", "num_of_item" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDERS" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-12-31') ), orders AS ( SELECT "user_id", "order_id", "product_id", "sale_price", "status" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDER_ITEMS" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-12-31') ), nest AS ( SELECT o."user_id", o."order_id", o."product_id", d."order_date", d."num_of_item", ROUND(o."sale_price", 2) AS "sale_price", ROUND(d."num_of_item" * o."sale_price", 2) AS "total_sale" FROM orders o INNER JOIN daate d ON o."order_id" = d."order_id" ORDER BY o."user_id" ), type AS ( SELECT "user_id", MIN(nest."order_date") AS "cohort_date", MAX(nest."order_date") AS "latest_shopping_date", DATEDIFF(MONTH, MIN(nest."order_date"), MAX(nest."order_date")) AS "lifespan_months", ROUND(SUM("total_sale"), 2) AS "ltv", COUNT("order_id") AS "no_of_order" FROM nest GROUP BY "user_id" ), kite AS ( SELECT m."user_id", m."email", m."gender", m."country", m."traffic_source", EXTRACT(YEAR FROM n."cohort_date") AS "cohort_year", n."latest_shopping_date", n."lifespan_months", n."ltv", n."no_of_order", ROUND(n."ltv" / n."no_of_order", 2) AS "avg_order_value" FROM main m INNER JOIN type n ON m."user_id" = n."user_id" ) SELECT "email" FROM kite ORDER BY "avg_order_value" DESC LIMIT 10;

input.natural_language_query: Please generate a report that, for each month in 2021, provides the number of orders, the number of unique purchasers, and the profit (calculated as the sum of product retail prices minus the sum of product costs), where the orders were placed during 2021 by users who registered in 2021 for inventory items created in 2021, and group the results by the users' country, product department, and product category.

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH orders_x_order_items AS ( SELECT orders.*, order_items."inventory_item_id", order_items."sale_price" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDERS" AS orders LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDER_ITEMS" AS order_items ON orders."order_id" = order_items."order_id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ), orders_x_inventory AS ( SELECT orders_x_order_items.*, inventory_items."product_category", inventory_items."product_department", inventory_items."product_retail_price", inventory_items."product_distribution_center_id", inventory_items."cost", distribution_centers."name" FROM orders_x_order_items LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."INVENTORY_ITEMS" AS inventory_items ON orders_x_order_items."inventory_item_id" = inventory_items."id" LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."DISTRIBUTION_CENTERS" AS distribution_centers ON inventory_items."product_distribution_center_id" = distribution_centers."id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(inventory_items."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ), orders_x_users AS ( SELECT orders_x_inventory.*, users."country" AS "users_country" FROM orders_x_inventory LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" AS users ON orders_x_inventory."user_id" = users."id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(users."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ) SELECT DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', TO_DATE(TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders_x_users."created_at" / 1000000))) AS "reporting_month", orders_x_users."users_country", orders_x_users."product_department", orders_x_users."product_category", COUNT(DISTINCT orders_x_users."order_id") AS "n_order", COUNT(DISTINCT orders_x_users."user_id") AS "n_purchasers", SUM(orders_x_users."product_retail_price") - SUM(orders_x_users."cost") AS "profit" FROM orders_x_users GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4 ORDER BY "reporting_month";

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH acs_2018 AS ( SELECT geo_id, median_income AS median_income_2018 FROM `bigquery-public-data.census_bureau_acs.censustract_2018_5yr` ), acs_2015 AS ( SELECT geo_id, median_income AS median_income_2015 FROM `bigquery-public-data.census_bureau_acs.censustract_2015_5yr` ), acs_diff AS ( SELECT a18.geo_id, a18.median_income_2018, a15.median_income_2015, (a18.median_income_2018 - a15.median_income_2015) AS median_income_diff, FROM acs_2018 a18 JOIN acs_2015 a15 ON a18.geo_id = a15.geo_id ), max_geo_id AS ( SELECT geo_id FROM acs_diff WHERE median_income_diff IS NOT NULL AND acs_diff.geo_id in ( SELECT geo_id FROM `bigquery-public-data.geo_census_tracts.census_tracts_california` ) ORDER BY median_income_diff DESC LIMIT 1 ) SELECT tracts.tract_ce as tract_code FROM max_geo_id JOIN `bigquery-public-data.geo_census_tracts.census_tracts_california` AS tracts ON max_geo_id.geo_id = tracts.geo_id;

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH main AS ( SELECT "id" AS "user_id", "email", "gender", "country", "traffic_source" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-12-31') ), daate AS ( SELECT "user_id", "order_id", CAST(TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) AS DATE) AS "order_date", "num_of_item" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDERS" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-12-31') ), orders AS ( SELECT "user_id", "order_id", "product_id", "sale_price", "status" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDER_ITEMS" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP("created_at" / 1000000.0) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP('2019-12-31') ), nest AS ( SELECT o."user_id", o."order_id", o."product_id", d."order_date", d."num_of_item", ROUND(o."sale_price", 2) AS "sale_price", ROUND(d."num_of_item" * o."sale_price", 2) AS "total_sale" FROM orders o INNER JOIN daate d ON o."order_id" = d."order_id" ORDER BY o."user_id" ), type AS ( SELECT "user_id", MIN(nest."order_date") AS "cohort_date", MAX(nest."order_date") AS "latest_shopping_date", DATEDIFF(MONTH, MIN(nest."order_date"), MAX(nest."order_date")) AS "lifespan_months", ROUND(SUM("total_sale"), 2) AS "ltv", COUNT("order_id") AS "no_of_order" FROM nest GROUP BY "user_id" ), kite AS ( SELECT m."user_id", m."email", m."gender", m."country", m."traffic_source", EXTRACT(YEAR FROM n."cohort_date") AS "cohort_year", n."latest_shopping_date", n."lifespan_months", n."ltv", n."no_of_order", ROUND(n."ltv" / n."no_of_order", 2) AS "avg_order_value" FROM main m INNER JOIN type n ON m."user_id" = n."user_id" ) SELECT "email" FROM kite ORDER BY "avg_order_value" DESC LIMIT 10;

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH orders_x_order_items AS ( SELECT orders.*, order_items."inventory_item_id", order_items."sale_price" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDERS" AS orders LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDER_ITEMS" AS order_items ON orders."order_id" = order_items."order_id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ), orders_x_inventory AS ( SELECT orders_x_order_items.*, inventory_items."product_category", inventory_items."product_department", inventory_items."product_retail_price", inventory_items."product_distribution_center_id", inventory_items."cost", distribution_centers."name" FROM orders_x_order_items LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."INVENTORY_ITEMS" AS inventory_items ON orders_x_order_items."inventory_item_id" = inventory_items."id" LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."DISTRIBUTION_CENTERS" AS distribution_centers ON inventory_items."product_distribution_center_id" = distribution_centers."id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(inventory_items."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ), orders_x_users AS ( SELECT orders_x_inventory.*, users."country" AS "users_country" FROM orders_x_inventory LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" AS users ON orders_x_inventory."user_id" = users."id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(users."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ) SELECT DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', TO_DATE(TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders_x_users."created_at" / 1000000))) AS "reporting_month", orders_x_users."users_country", orders_x_users."product_department", orders_x_users."product_category", COUNT(DISTINCT orders_x_users."order_id") AS "n_order", COUNT(DISTINCT orders_x_users."user_id") AS "n_purchasers", SUM(orders_x_users."product_retail_price") - SUM(orders_x_users."cost") AS "profit" FROM orders_x_users GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4 ORDER BY "reporting_month";

searches.query: monthly average balance MAB calculation zero balance account banking methodology
searches.rationale: The task's external knowledge concerns MAB calculations and zero-balance handling, so I confirmed how MAB is computed and how negative or nil balances are treated in retail banking.
searches.context_summary: Monthly Average Balance (MAB) is calculated as the sum of an account's daily closing balances divided by the number of days in the month, so it averages many point-in-time daily balances rather than reading a single snapshot. Banks set an MAB requirement as the minimum average balance a customer must maintain, and a shortfall on some days can be offset by holding a higher balance on others, giving MAB more flexibility than a strict daily-minimum rule. Zero-balance accounts waive the MAB requirement entirely, letting holders keep a nil balance without penalty, though usually with fewer features than minimum-balance accounts. Non-maintenance of the required MAB triggers penalties that vary by bank, account type, and whether the branch is urban or rural. These sources ground the distinction between a daily-average MAB and a start-of-month, point-in-time balance snapshot, and they clarify standard zero-balance handling, supporting interpretations that contrast previous-month point-in-time totals with sustained daily-average performance and that treat a negative-to-zero replacement rule as a deliberate methodological choice.

searches.rationale: The task hinges on average daily balance methodology and carrying balances forward, so I sought the standard definition and calculation used in banking.
searches.context_summary: The average daily balance (ADB) method computes a figure by summing the account balance for each day in a period and dividing by the number of days in that period. Because every day in the cycle must contribute a balance, the running balance is carried forward on days with no new transactions, exactly the forward-fill logic the task describes. Banks and credit-card issuers favor ADB precisely because it captures balance fluctuations throughout the period rather than a single snapshot, and interest is then charged as (APR x days in cycle x ADB) / 365. Alternative approaches such as the beginning-balance and adjusted-balance methods ignore intra-period movement and are considered less accurate. This established methodology of carrying forward and aggregating daily balances is the external knowledge that grounds the task's construction, though the task substitutes monthly maximum daily balances (with negatives floored to zero) for the traditional average to build a peak-exposure metric. That distinction, using maximums rather than averages, is what separates a routine reporting exercise from a liquidity-peak and aggregate-exposure interpretation.

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH station_neighborhoods AS ( SELECT bs.station_id, bs.name AS station_name, nb.neighborhood FROM `bigquery-public-data.san_francisco.bikeshare_stations` bs JOIN bigquery-public-data.san_francisco_neighborhoods.boundaries nb ON ST_Intersects(ST_GeogPoint(bs.longitude, bs.latitude), nb.neighborhood_geom) ), neighborhood_crime_counts AS ( SELECT neighborhood, COUNT(*) AS crime_count FROM ( SELECT n.neighborhood FROM bigquery-public-data.san_francisco.sfpd_incidents i JOIN bigquery-public-data.san_francisco_neighborhoods.boundaries n ON ST_Intersects(ST_GeogPoint(i.longitude, i.latitude), n.neighborhood_geom) ) AS incident_neighborhoods GROUP BY neighborhood ) SELECT sn.neighborhood, COUNT(station_name) AS station_number, ANY_VALUE(ncc.crime_count) AS crime_number FROM station_neighborhoods sn JOIN neighborhood_crime_counts ncc ON sn.neighborhood = ncc.neighborhood GROUP BY sn.neighborhood ORDER BY crime_number ASC

input.natural_language_query: Please generate a report that, for each month in 2021, provides the number of orders, the number of unique purchasers, and the profit (calculated as the sum of product retail prices minus the sum of product costs), where the orders were placed during 2021 by users who registered in 2021 for inventory items created in 2021, and group the results by the users' country, product department, and product category.

gold_subtasks.expected_SQL: WITH orders_x_order_items AS ( SELECT orders.*, order_items."inventory_item_id", order_items."sale_price" FROM "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDERS" AS orders LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."ORDER_ITEMS" AS order_items ON orders."order_id" = order_items."order_id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ), orders_x_inventory AS ( SELECT orders_x_order_items.*, inventory_items."product_category", inventory_items."product_department", inventory_items."product_retail_price", inventory_items."product_distribution_center_id", inventory_items."cost", distribution_centers."name" FROM orders_x_order_items LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."INVENTORY_ITEMS" AS inventory_items ON orders_x_order_items."inventory_item_id" = inventory_items."id" LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."DISTRIBUTION_CENTERS" AS distribution_centers ON inventory_items."product_distribution_center_id" = distribution_centers."id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(inventory_items."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ), orders_x_users AS ( SELECT orders_x_inventory.*, users."country" AS "users_country" FROM orders_x_inventory LEFT JOIN "THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."THELOOK_ECOMMERCE"."USERS" AS users ON orders_x_inventory."user_id" = users."id" WHERE TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(users."created_at" / 1000000) BETWEEN TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-01-01') AND TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ('2021-12-31') ) SELECT DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', TO_DATE(TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ(orders_x_users."created_at" / 1000000))) AS "reporting_month", orders_x_users."users_country", orders_x_users."product_department", orders_x_users."product_category", COUNT(DISTINCT orders_x_users."order_id") AS "n_order", COUNT(DISTINCT orders_x_users."user_id") AS "n_purchasers", SUM(orders_x_users."product_retail_price") - SUM(orders_x_users."cost") AS "profit" FROM orders_x_users GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4 ORDER BY "reporting_month";

options.B: The reporting requirements are basic and can be handled by any standard business intelligence tool without consideration of the technical complexities involved in cross-system data integration
